title: Cu/Cu2O Interconnected Porous Aerogel Catalyst for Highly Productive Electrosynthesis of Ethanol from CO2
abstract: Use of Cu and Cu+ is one of the most promising approaches for the production of C2 products by the electrocatalytic CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR) because it can facilitate CO2 activation and CC dimerization. However, the selective electrosynthesis of C2+ products on Cu0Cu+ interfaces is critically limited due to the low electrocatalytic production of ethanol relative to ethylene. In this study, a novel porous Cu/Cu2O aerogel network is introduced to afford high ethanol productivity by the electrocatalytic CO2RR. The aerogel is synthesized by a simple chemical redox reaction of a precursor and a reducing agent. CO2RR results reveal that the Cu/Cu2O aerogel produces ethanol as the major product, exhibiting a Faradaic efficiency (FEEtOH) of 41.2% and a partial current density (JEtOH) of 32.55 mA cm−2 in an H-cell reactor. This is the best electrosynthesis performance for ethanol production reported thus far. Electron microscopy and electrochemical analysis results reveal that this dramatic increase in the electrosynthesis performance for ethanol can be attributed to a large number of Cu0Cu+ interfaces and an increase of the local pH in the confined porous aerogel network structure with a high-surface-area.

Use of Cu and Cu+ is one of the most promising approaches for the production of C2 products by the electrocatalytic CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR) because it can facilitate CO2 activation and CC dimerization. However, the selective electrosynthesis of C2+ products on Cu0Cu+ interfaces is critically limited due to the low electrocatalytic production of ethanol relative to ethylene. In this study, a novel porous Cu/Cu2O aerogel network is introduced to afford high ethanol productivity by the electrocatalytic CO2RR. The aerogel is synthesized by a simple chemical redox reaction of a precursor and a reducing agent. CO2RR results reveal that the Cu/Cu2O aerogel produces ethanol as the major product, exhibiting a Faradaic efficiency (FEEtOH) of 41.2% and a partial current density (JEtOH) of 32.55 mA cm−2 in an H-cell reactor. This is the best electrosynthesis performance for ethanol production reported thus far. Electron microscopy and electrochemical analysis results reveal that this dramatic increase in the electrosynthesis performance for ethanol can be attributed to a large number of Cu0Cu+ interfaces and an increase of the local pH in the confined porous aerogel network structure with a high-surface-area.

1. Introduction
Electrocatalytic CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR) has attracted considerable attention due to the generation of multi-carbon products (C2+), such as ethylene and ethanol, which exhibit high energy densities; hence, these products are useful for renewable electricity storage as well as feedstock for chemical production.[1,2] Various approaches, including the control of the Cu nanostructure,[3,4] use of Cu-based polyelements,[5] and surface oxidation of Cu-based catalysts,[6] have been employed to enhance the Faradaic efficiency (FE) and partial current density of C2+ products (JC2+). Among these methods, modulation of the surface oxidation state using oxide-derived Cu is particularly interesting because interfaces between Cu+ and Cu0 regions promote CC dimerization while simultaneously impeding the C1 product
pathway.[7–11] Thus far, this approach is known to afford the highest FEC2+ and JC2+ values.
However, the selective electrosynthesis of C2+ products on Cu exhibits limitations, including a low selectivity for producing ethanol relative to ethylene. The production of liquid ethanol (EtOH) from carbon dioxide (CO2) is highly desirable because EtOH can be used to store and transport renewable energy due to its higher energy density than those of other gas products.[12] FEEtOH and partial current density (JEtOH) are limited due to the competitive hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) and the adverse binding energy of reaction intermediates in the CO2RR on a small surface area.[2,13] Several approaches have been reported to enhance the selectivity and productivity of ethanol, including the fabrication of Cu+Cu0 interfaces using an oxide or a dopant[8,9,14] or the use of a multicomponent catalyst[15–17] that can control the binding energy. For example, boron-doped or nitride-derived Cu and Cu+ species have been reported to exhibit FEEtOH values of 27 and 19% with JEtOH values of 18.9 and 4.16  mA cm−2, respectively. In addition, O2 plasma treatment on Cu nanocube surfaces leads to a FEEtOH of 22% and a JEtOH of 11 mA cm−2; this increase was attributed to the Cu+ species that were stabilized by the presence of residual oxygen. Despite advances in the field that have generated high yields of the C2+ product, achieving high electrosynthesis performance for the production of ethanol relative to ethylene remains a challenge; it has been very difficult to achieve both high selectivity and productivity to EtOH at the same time. In this study, a porous Cu/Cu2O aerogel network was introduced for the electrosynthesis of EtOH as the major product from CO2 with a high JEtOH. A large number of Cu0Cu+ interfaces in confined spaces with a high-surface-area resulted in a high EtOH electrosynthesis performance. The resulting Cu/ Cu2O aerogel exhibited not only a high FEEtOH (FEC2  ≈ 80.8% and FEEtOH ≈ 41.2%) but also a high JEtOH (≈32.55 mA cm−2) in an H-cell. These results represent the highest EtOH electrosynthesis performance reported thus far. Moreover, the Cu/Cu2O aerogel was applied in a flow-cell reactor as a gas diffusion electrode (GDE), and the system exhibited a high energy efficiency (EE) for EtOH production at 26.3%.

sections.heading: 2. Results and Discussion
sections.text:
Figure 1a shows the overall scheme for the fabrication of porous Cu/Cu2O aerogel networks for the high production of C2 products by electrocatalytic CO2RR. The Cu/Cu2O aerogel was prepared by a simple wet chemical redox reaction in an aqueous solution at room temperature.[18] An aqueous CuCl2 precursor solution was mixed by vigorous stirring under Ar atmosphere, followed by the addition of NaOH. As the reducing agent, NaBH4 in various amounts was injected into the precursor solution which had a transparent light blue color to control the average oxidation state of the porous aerogel. Cu/Cu2O aerogel samples were prepared with five different oxidation states. When an excess amount (9  mm) of NaBH4 was used, a Cu2O aerogel with a Cu core covered by Cu2O was obtained. The resulting products, which were black in color, were collected after several cycles of centrifugation in water and dried at room temperature (Figure S1, Supporting Information).
To determine the surface ratio of the Cu+ species and the average oxidation state of the porous aerogels, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) and X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) at the Cu K-edge were obtained. The ratio of the Cu+ species on the surface was investigated using Auger Cu LMM peaks: Cu+ and Cu0 peaks were located at 916 and 919.9 eV, respectively (Figure  1b, Figure S2, Supporting Information).[9,19,20] The surface Cu+ species on the Cu/Cu2O aerogels varied from 10.2 to 36.1%, depending on the amount of NaBH4 used during synthesis. Other elements except for Cu and O, such as sodium, boron, and chlorine were not detected from XPS which means the absence of incorporated elements in Cu and Cu2O (Figure S3, Supporting Information). The Cu2O aerogel contained only 42.4% of Cu+ because the penetrating X-ray could detect the core Cu0 species. The absorption edge of the XANES spectrum linearly increased from 8979 eV for Cu0 to 8980.5 eV for Cu+ (Figure 1c).[8,9] All absorption edges for the Cu/Cu2O aerogels were located between the edges of Cu0 and Cu+ (Figure S4, Supporting Information). In particular, the Cu/Cu2O aerogel with 21.6% Cu+ at the surface and the Cu2O aerogel exhibited average oxidation states of 0.26 and 0.40 with absorption edges at 8979.4 and 8980.1  eV, respectively. Thus, by controlling the amount of NaBH4 as the reducing agent during synthesis, the surface Cu+ species and the average oxidation state of the Cu/Cu2O aerogel could be tuned.
Figure  1d shows a representative scanning electron microscopy (SEM) image of the Cu/Cu2O aerogel with 21.6% Cu+. The aerogel structure was uniformly formed on a carbon paper electrode, which exhibited an interconnected network structure with nanoscale pores.[18,21] High-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) images further confirmed that the Cu/Cu2O aerogel nanoparticles, exhibiting diameters of about 50  nm, are interconnected (Figure  1e). In fact, numerous gaps between the nanoparticle networks can act as pores, which play a pivotal role for effectively promoting electrocatalytic CO2RR for the formation of ethanol by providing intermediate confinement and the local pH effect, as discussed later. The surface area of the aerogel network structure was determined by electrochemical surface area (ECSA) measurements (Figure  1f). The ECSA was linearly related to the corresponding capacitance (CdI), which was determined by cyclic voltammetry (CV) at scan rates ranging from 25 to 200 mV s−1.[22] The CdI values of the Cu/Cu2O aerogel with 21.6% Cu+ and the Cu2O aerogel were measured as 5.21 and 6.46 mF cm−2, which were 23.2 and 28.8 times greater than that of the Cu film (0.224 mF cm−2), respectively (Figure S5, Supporting Information). Therefore, our Cu/Cu2O aerogel exhibits a ≈23.2 times greater electrochemically active surface area than that of the film due to its porous aerogel network structure.
The Cu0Cu+ interface density, which is important in the electrocatalytic reduction of CO2 to the C2 product,[7,8] was determined by measuring the Cu and Cu2O domain sizes by X-ray diffraction (XRD) spectra (Figure  2a). Dominant XRD peaks located at 2θ  = 36.4°, 42.2°, and 61.6° corresponded to the Cu2O(111), Cu(111), and Cu(200), respectively.[23] With the increase in the surface Cu+ species from 10.2 to 36.1% in different amounts of NaBH4, peak intensities of Cu2O increased, indicating changes in the Cu/Cu2O ratio. The domain sizes

of Cu and Cu2O were measured by analyzing the full-width at half-maximum of the XRD peaks for dominant Cu(111) and Cu2O(111) using the Scherrer equation in samples with various Cu/Cu2O ratios (Figure 2b, Table S1, Supporting Information). The results reveal that the mean domain sizes of Cu2O(111) and Cu(111) remain almost constant at ≈5.3 and 8.3  nm, respectively, regardless of changes in the Cu/Cu2O ratio. Thus, our Cu/Cu2O aerogels comprise nanometer-sized crystalline Cu and Cu2O with controlled average oxidation states, enabling to generate a large number of Cu0Cu+ interfaces.
To further confirm the Cu0Cu+ interfaces from Cu and Cu2O domains, the surface lattice was investigated by HRTEM imaging and fast Fourier transform (FFT) (Figure  2c). The lattice spacings of 0.179, 0.209, and 0.245  nm in the HRTEM image corresponded to the Cu(200), Cu(111), and Cu2O(111) facets, respectively. Interfaces between the Cu and Cu2O domains were clearly visible on the Cu/Cu2O aerogel surface. After carefully inspecting the image, the domain size of Cu and Cu2O was 5–10 nm, which was confirmed by the XRD result in Figure 2b.
HRTEM with inverse-FFT mapping reveals that the interfaces between the Cu and Cu2O components in the aerogel network structure are uniformly distributed. Figure 2d shows a representative inverse-FFT mapping image of the Cu/Cu2O aerogel network with 21.6% Cu+. In the images, red, green, and blue represent the Cu(200), Cu(111), and Cu2O(111) facets, respectively. Each crystal plane was well distributed in the Cu/ Cu2O aerogel. A small domain size of 5–10  nm for Cu and Cu2O was further confirmed on the overall Cu/Cu2O aerogel surface. Therefore, Cu0Cu+ interfaces could be densely located on the Cu/Cu2O surface from a good distribution of small Cu and Cu2O domains. However, Cu and Cu2O domains were not well distributed in Cu2O aerogels having 41.6% Cu+. Core-shell-like features were observed, in which the Cu2O domains were distinctly located in the shell, while the Cu domains were located in the core (Figure S6, Supporting Information).
Electrocatalytic CO2RR for the aerogel catalysts was evaluated after drop-casting the catalyst ink, prepared with a mixture of Nafion in a methanol solvent, on a carbon paper (Figure 3). The electrochemical test was performed in an H-cell reactor with a CO2-saturated 0.1 m KCl electrolyte as KCl is typically used for the stable preservation of oxidation states during reduction reactions.[8,19,24] Figure  3a shows the FE for the CO2RR products of the Cu/Cu2O aerogel with 21.6% Cu+ at an applied potential between −0.8 and −1.3 V with reference to the reversible hydrogen electrode (VRHE). The high FE for the C2 products was maintained over a wide potential window for more negative than −1.0 VRHE. The highest FEs at −1.1 VRHE for ethanol and ethylene were 41.2 and 39.6%, respectively. The generation of Cl chemicals, including CO and HCOOH, was significantly suppressed in this potential window, while C1 chemicals were the major products of CO2RR at less negative applied potentials. In addition, the HER decreased to an FE of ≈20%, leading to selective CO2RR at potentials more negative than −0.9 VRHE. The FEEtOH of Cu/Cu2O aerogels with different Cu+ ratios were compared at −1.1 VRHE to investigate the optimal oxidation state (Figure  3b). Regardless of the oxidation state changes, the aerogel structure and crystallite size
of Cu and Cu2O were almost identical (Figure  2b, Figure S7, Supporting Information). The Cu2O aerogel, which had a surface that was mostly covered by Cu+, exhibited a FEEtOH of only ≈20% due to the decreased number of Cu0Cu+ interfaces. The Cu/Cu2O aerogel with 21.6% Cu+ exhibited the highest FEEtOH (≈41%), which gradually dropped to ≈20% at 10% Cu+. Relationship between the abundance of Cu0Cu+ interfaces (calculated by summing the length of interfaces per area) and FEEtOH has been investigated in Figures S7 and S8, Supporting Information, showing a similar tendency of both maximized at Cu/Cu2O aerogel with 21.6% Cu+. This tendency could not be seen by using K2SO4 electrolyte with decreased FEEtOH to ≈20% by fast reduction of Cu+ (Figure S9, Supporting Information). Preservation of Cu+ species by chloride ion effect in KCl electrolyte played an important role during electrocatalytic CO2RR with Cu/Cu2O aerogel.
To demonstrate the novelty of the Cu/Cu2O aerogel catalyst, the CO2RR performance of the Cu/Cu2O aerogel was compared with those of the Cu2O film and Cu2O aerogel (Figure 3c, Figure S10, Supporting Information). Cu2O films were prepared by the thermal oxidation of the Cu film8, and Cu2O aerogels were formed by controlling the amount of NaBH4 in the precursor solutions of the aerogel catalyst. The Cu2O films exhibited a poor FEC2 (≈30%) at more negative potentials (−1.3 VRHE), and the FEEtOH was less than 20%. The Cu2O aerogel exhibited a moderate FEC2 (≈45%) at a less negative potential (−1.1 VRHE); however, the FEEtOH was still ≈20%, which was similar to that of the Cu2O film. Notably, the Cu/Cu2O aerogel exhibited high C2 selectivity, especially for ethanol production at an overall applied potential. These Cu/Cu2O aerogels exhibited an FEC2 of ≈81% and an FEEtOH of ≈41% at −1.1 VRHE, which were approximately two and four times greater than those for the Cu2O aerogels and Cu2O film.
The ratio of FEEtOH to FEC2H4 was calculated to evaluate the selectivity for the production of EtOH over C2H4 during CO2RR (Figure 3d). Similar to previously reported Cu catalysts, the Cu2O film and Cu2O aerogel produced C2H4 as the major product at −1.1 and −1.0 VRHE. Notably, our Cu/Cu2O aerogel exhibited a FEEtOH/FEC2H4 value greater than 1, indicating that EtOH is the major product from CO2RR. This reversal of selectivity for EtOH and ethylene may be attributed to the Cu0Cu+ interfaces in the confined structure, possibly resulting in a highly localized intermediate (CO) concentration and pH and subsequently facilitating in the EtOH formation.[15,16]
In addition, the C2/C1 product ratios for CO2RR at −1.1 VRHE were investigated using various catalysts (Figure S11, Supporting Information). The C2/C1 ratio of the Cu2O film was only 0.51 due to difficulties in the CC coupling reaction. The C2/ C1 ratio of our highly porous aerogel structure was significantly increased at 3.97 (Cu2O aerogel), which was another indication that the aerogel system provides an intermediate confinement and local pH effect.[3,25,26] Furthermore, the C2/C1 ratio reached 8.23 by the introduction of a well-mixed Cu/Cu2O surface. This could be related to a Cu0Cu+ interface effect that reduces the energy barrier for the CC coupling reaction.[7]
Very importantly, in addition to the selective formation of C2 and EtOH, the Cu/Cu2O aerogel exhibited a significantly enhanced JEtOH. Figure  3e shows the comparison of JEtOH between −0.9 and −1.2 VRHE. The JEtOH for the Cu/Cu2O aerogel

at −1.1 VRHE was 32.55  mA cm−2, which was 32.48 and 4.90 times greater than those for the Cu2O film and Cu2O aerogel, respectively. The high surface area formed by the porous network and the dense population of Cu0Cu+ interfaces played important roles in the significant enhancement of the JEtOH. In addition, the Cu/Cu2O aerogel exhibited a stable performance, with 80.1 and 95% retention of its initial FEEtOH and JEtOH, respectively, during an electrolysis time of 5 h (Figure S12, Supporting Information). After the electrolysis in the KCl electrolyte, despite slight changes in morphology, such as the aggregation and sintering of the aerogel structure, the oxidation states and Cu0Cu+ interfaces did not change significantly (Figure S13, Supporting Information).
The Cu/Cu2O aerogel was applied to a flow-cell reactor using a GDE (Figure  4). The Cu/Cu2O aerogel was deposited on a hydrophobic polytetrafluoroethylene-coated carbon paper. The reaction in the GDE cell occurred at the triple-phase boundary among the CO2 gas that diffused through the microporous carbon nanofiber, the liquid electrolyte wetted on the hydrophobic layer, and the solid catalyst (Figure 4a).[27,28] Notably, the high porosity of the Cu/Cu2O aerogels is advantageous for the efficient mass transport of gaseous products generated at the triple-phase reaction site and to prevent the interference of bubbles.[29] The EE of ethanol production using Cu deposited by an E-beam was compared. The FE and EE for ethanol reached ≈45 and ≈26% in the GDE cell with the Cu/Cu2O aerogel at −0.7 VRHE, respectively (Figure  4b). Moreover, the onset potential for ethanol production has been shifted to more positive potential by using GDE cell which is derived by the generation of high local OH– concentration without neutralization of carbonation effect and increase of reactant concentration.[15,27] A JEtOH of 72.1 mA cm−2 was achieved on Cu/Cu2O in the GDE cell, corresponding to a sixfold enhancement over Cu in the GDE cell (Figure  4c). This high ethanol productivity is attributed to the synergistic effect of the inherent properties of the efficient Cu/Cu2O aerogel catalysts and the systematic advantage of flow-cell reactors. As our Cu/Cu2O aerogel exhibited the highest productivity for the electrosynthesis of EtOH, our catalyst was expected to achieve higher EE and J values through the optimization of the GDE cell.

Figure 5a shows the EtOH electrosynthesis performance for the recently reported electrocatalysts in H-cells. Most of the catalysts, including boron-doped Cu, Cu on nitride, and plasmaactivated Cu nanocubes, exhibited FEEtOH and JEtOH values of less than 30% and 20 mA cm−2, respectively. Dopant or nitrideand oxide-derived catalysts enhanced ethanol selectivity with high C2+ selectivity by facilitating CC dimerization and CO2 activation for densely packed Cu0 and Cu+ species. Previous studies also have reported that productivity is enhanced by the increase in both selectivity for C2+ products, including EtOH,

and the surface area using nanoparticle structures or rough surfaces.[4,8–10] To best of our knowledge, the EtOH electrosynthesis performance of our Cu/Cu2O aerogel, with a FEEtOH of 41.2% and a JEtOH of 32.55 mA cm−2, is the highest reported value for the electrocatalytic CO2 reduction in H-cells (Figure 5a).
Unlike previous catalysts with nanoparticle or planar film structures, our aerogel catalyst exhibited several unique features. First, our aerogel exhibited an interconnected network structure that could produce several confined areas in the catalyst, a feature that typically increases local pH effects. A recent study has reported that the local pH and CO concentration around Cu can increase the selectivity for produced EtOH compared to ethylene.[15,25,30] Therefore, the confined geometry of the aerogel structure plays an important role in enhancing the selectivity of EtOH relative to ethylene. In addition, the aerogel structure exhibited extremely high surface areas with a good distribution of small Cu/Cu2O domains. Therefore, the number of Cu0Cu+ interfaces could be significantly increased, thereby enhancing the JEtOH.
To verify the effect of the local pH in the confined space of the aerogel structure, CO2RR was conducted in various electrolytes with different buffer strengths: 0.1 m K2PO4, 0.1 m KHCO3, and 0.1 m KClO4 (Figure 5b). FEEtOH decreased in the presence of K2PO4 and KHCO3, which exhibited strong and moderate buffer strengths, respectively. These species neutralized the hydroxide ion (OH–) in solution, which canceled the local pH effect. On the other hand, in electrolytes without a buffering effect (KClO4 and KCl), a high FEEtOH was maintained due to the generation of a high local pH in the aerogel structure. The FEH2 decreased to 35% for the Cu2O aerogel, and it decreased further at 17.3% for the Cu/Cu2O aerogel. This dramatic suppression of HER was caused by the local pH increase in the confined space of the aerogel structure. In addition, high selectivity for the production of EtOH relative to ethylene could be derived from the localized concentration of CO around Cu/ Cu2O in the confined structure.[15]
The electrochemical analysis results reveal that the selective formation of EtOH in the Cu/Cu2O aerogel is related to intrinsic catalytic activity. Linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) reveals a considerably higher current density for the Cu/Cu2O aerogel compared to the control samples throughout the potential range (Figure S14, Supporting Information). In addition, the onset potential for the Cu/Cu2O aerogel was −0.398 VRHE, which was more positive than those for the other materials (−0.488 V, −0.623  V, and −0.658 VRHE for the Cu2O aerogel, Cu2O film, and Cu film, respectively). In addition, Arrhenius plots were constructed to investigate the overall activation energy, which was calculated from the absolute value of the slope (Figure S15, Supporting Information). The absolute value of the slope for the Cu/Cu2O aerogel was 2.61, which was 1.65 times less than that for the Cu film; this result could be explained by the high intrinsic electrochemical activity. Furthermore, Tafel plots were constructed by using JEtOH to explore its effect on the kinetics of ethanol production (Figure S16, Supporting Information).[8] The Tafel slopes were 68.9, 80.1, 128, and 132  mV dec−1 for the Cu/Cu2O aerogel, Cu2O aerogel, Cu2O film, and Cu film, respectively, implying a change in the overall rate-determining step. From previous studies, similar slopes were observed for CO reduction (CO to C2 products, 68.9 mV dec−1) and the first electron-transfer step in CO2 reduction (CO2  + e ⟶ CO2–,
132 mV  dec−1).[27,31] This result implies that our Cu/Cu2O aerogel may change the rate-determining steps, a phenomenon that is not completely understood thus far.
From ECSA and TEM results, the Cu/Cu2O aerogel exhibited a 23.2 times higher surface area, with a uniform distribution of small Cu and Cu2O domains. From these results, our catalyst exhibits a large number of Cu0Cu+ interfaces. This might be the main origin for high JEtOH in electrosynthesis from CO2 using our Cu/Cu2O aerogel.
We summarized the origins of enhanced ethanol electrosynthesis on Cu/Cu2O aerogel in Figure  5c. First, the high surface area provided abundant reaction sites for CO2RR. Second, the porous structure of the Cu/Cu2O aerogel accumulated the reaction intermediates and hydroxide ions. High local concentrations of C1 intermediates in confined structures promoted further reactions by C–C dimerization, promoting the selectivity for EtOH relative to ethylene. In addition, the local increase in pH-induced slow proton adsorption kinetics, which suppressed HER. Finally, the densely located Cu0Cu+ interfaces played key roles in CC dimerization as the adsorbed CO on Cu0 and Cu+ exhibited an opposite charge.

sections.heading: 3. Conclusion
sections.text: In summary, a Cu/Cu2O aerogel catalyst was developed for the electrosynthesis of ethanol from CO2. The Cu/Cu2O aerogel exhibited high productivity (JEtOH = 32.55 mA cm−2) and selectivity to C2 products (FEEtOH ≈ 41.2%, FEC2H4 ≈ 39.6%) at −1.1 V RHE. The dense distribution of the Cu0Cu+ interfaces on the porous aerogel and the high surface area played a crucial role in enhancing the electrocatalytic CO2RR performance. Furthermore, the possibility of applying the material in a GDE flow cell was explored, and a high JEtOH for the Cu/Cu2O aerogel was obtained (72.1 mA cm−2). This aerogel electrocatalyst is thought to be an appealing model for the commercial electrosynthesis of ethanol from CO2.

sections.heading: 4. Experimental Section
sections.text:
Synthesis of the Cu/Cu2O and Cu2O Aerogels: First, 150 mL of distilled (DI) water was purged by nitrogen in sealed round flask for 30 min. Second, 15 mL of CuCl2 (0.1 m) and 15 mL of NaOH (0.2 m) were added under vigorous stirring with maintaining purging. After 30 min of stabilization, 150 µL of ethanol and a controlled amount of NaBH4 in 25 mL of DI water were rapidly added into this solution. The mass of the added NaBH4 was 12.5, 25, 37.5, 50, 62.5, or 70 mg for the five Cu/Cu2O aerogels, respectively, as well as the Cu2O aerogel. After 30  min, the mixture was centrifuged and rinsed several times with water, resulting in a black powder. These samples were dried under vacuum overnight.
Preparation of the Cu and Cu2O Films: The Cu film was prepared by the potentiostatic electropolishing of a copper foil in phosphoric acid (85% in water) at 2.1  V versus the counter electrode. The Cu2O film electrodes were fabricated by electrodeposition at −0.25 V versus RHE in 0.5 m CuSO4 with lactic acid and 5 m NaOH.
Preparation of the Working Electrode: The catalyst ink was prepared by dispersing 10  mg of the sample powder in a 1  mL methanol solution containing 20 µL Nafion (5%). The solution was ultrasonicated for 1 h. Then, 71 µL of the catalyst ink was drop-casted on a 1-cm2 carbon paper and dried for 6 h.

Electrochemical Measurements: Electrochemical tests were performed in an H-cell reactor comprising two compartments and a protonexchange membrane. First, 50  mL of the electrolyte (0.1 m KCl, 0.1 m K2PO4, 0.1 m KHCO3, or 0.1 m KClO4) was injected into each compartment and purged with CO2 gas for 30 min before CO2 reduction. Pt coil and an Ag/AgCl (3 m KCl saturated) electrode were used as the counter and reference electrodes, respectively. First, the working electrode was electrochemically reduced by cyclic voltammetry (CV) between −0.5 and −2.0 V versus RHE at a rate of 0.1 V s−1 for five cycles. CO2RR was performed with chrono-amperometry (CA) measurement at each fixed potential for 30  min. During constant potential with iR correction, the gas products were detected by gas chromatography (Agilent 7890 GC), which was connected to the reactor. Liquid products were quantified using 1H nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR Bruker AVANCE III HD). After electrolysis, 630 µL of electrolyte was mixed with 70 µL of deuterated water (D2O), 35 µL of 50 mm phenol, and 10 mm DMSO for reference. Calculation for ethanol energy conversion efficiency (EE) was calculated for the half-cell in the cathode. The ethanol EE can be calculated using the following equation:

The overpotential of oxygen evolution was assumed to be zero, and Eethanol  = 0.09 VRHE for CO2RR. Eapplied is the potential used in the experiment. FEethanol is the calculated FE to ethanol in percentage.
Flow-Cell Reactor Electrolysis: Carbon paper with a microporous layer (Sigracet 39 BC, Fuel cell store) was used as a gas diffusion electrode (GDE). E-beam-evaporated Pt on GDE was used as the counter electrode, and Ag/AgCl was used as the working electrode. CO2 electrolysis was tested in a flow-cell reactor comprising polyetheretherketone and a silicone gasket for sealing. The gas flow rate was controlled at 10 sccm using a mass-flow controller. CO2 gas flowing at the backside of the cathode GDE was connected to the GC, and the backside of the anode GDE was exposed to air. The catholyte and anolyte were separated, and the flow rate was 2 mL min−1. 1 m KCl was used as the electrolyte with a Nafion proton-exchange membrane.
Characterization: The samples were characterized by scanning microscopy (FEI Magellan 400), transmission electron microscopy (Tecnai G2 F30), XRD (Rigaku SmartLab), and XPS (Axis-Supra). Inversefast Fourier transformation (Inverse-FFT) mapping was conducted from the FFT data using Gatan Digital Microscopy 3. The double-layer capacitance measurement for ECSA was conducted by CV in a 0.1 m KCl electrolyte, which was determined by the value of the slope of the linear fits and was proportional to the ECSA.
